subject: Computer Science
summary: Object-oriented concepts and how C++ and Java implement them: classes, constructors, inheritance, overloading, virtual functions, templates and exceptions, plus Java's JVM, data types, packages, interfaces and threads. DSSSB asks many statement-based and output-tracing questions here, so exact rules and outputs matter.

sections.heading: OOP concepts: the object model
sections.body:
**OOP** organises a program around **objects** (data plus the functions that operate on it) instead of procedures. A **class** is a blueprint (user-defined type); an **object** is an instance of a class.
Core features:
- **Encapsulation**: wrapping data and functions into a single unit (the class). With access control it gives **data hiding**.
- **Abstraction**: showing only essential features and hiding implementation details (abstract classes, interfaces).
- **Inheritance**: a derived (sub) class acquires the properties of a base (super) class, giving **reusability**.
- **Polymorphism**: "one name, many forms"; the same message produces different behaviour (overloading, overriding).
- **Dynamic binding**: the function body to execute is chosen at run time.
- **Message passing**: objects communicate by calling each other's methods.
**Encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism** are the three concepts every OO language must support; abstraction is often added as a fourth.
**Simula 67** is regarded as the first OO language and **Smalltalk** as a pure OO language. C++ is hybrid (procedural code is still allowed); Java is not "pure" OO because it has primitive types.

rows: Data moves freely between functions (global data)
Data hidden inside objects; accessed through methods
Examples: Simula, Smalltalk, C++, Java, C#, Python

sections.heading: Classes, objects, access specifiers and static members (C++)
sections.body:
A C++ class contains **data members** and **member functions**. Access is controlled by three **access specifiers**:
- `private`: accessible only inside the class (and by its friends). **Default for `class`.**
- `protected`: like private, but also accessible in derived classes.
- `public`: accessible from anywhere. **Default for `struct`.**
Member functions defined inside the class body are implicitly **inline**. A function defined outside uses the **scope resolution operator** `::`, e.g. `void Box::show() { ... }`.
Every non-static member function receives a hidden pointer **`this`** pointing to the calling object.
A **static data member** is shared by all objects (one copy per class) and must be defined once outside the class. A **static member function** can access only static members, has no `this` pointer and can be called as `Class::func()`.
A **friend function** is not a member, yet it can access private and protected members. Friendship is not inherited, not symmetric and not transitive.
The size of an empty class object in C++ is **1 byte** (so that every object has a distinct address).

sections.heading: Constructors and destructors
sections.body:
A **constructor** has the same name as the class, has **no return type (not even void)** and is called automatically when an object is created. Types:
- **Default constructor**: takes no arguments. If you write no constructor at all, the compiler supplies one; once you write any constructor, the implicit default one is not generated.
- **Parameterized constructor**: takes arguments, e.g. `Point(int x, int y)`.
- **Copy constructor**: `Point(const Point &p)`. The parameter must be a **reference**; pass-by-value would itself need a copy and recurse forever. It is invoked when an object is initialised from another object, passed by value or returned by value.
Constructors can be **overloaded** and can have default arguments, but they **cannot be virtual, static or inherited**.
A **destructor** `~ClassName()` takes no arguments and returns nothing, so there is only **one per class** (no overloading). It **can be virtual**. It is called automatically when the object goes out of scope or is deleted.
**Order of calls:** base-class constructor first, then member objects, then the derived constructor body. Destructors run in exactly the **reverse** order. Local objects are destroyed in reverse order of creation.

sections.heading: Inheritance: types and visibility modes
sections.body:
**Inheritance** creates a new class from an existing one: `class Derived : access-mode Base { ... };`
Types of inheritance:
- **Single**: one base, one derived.
- **Multiple**: one derived class from two or more bases (`class C : public A, public B`). Supported in C++, **not for classes in Java**.
- **Multilevel**: A → B → C.
- **Hierarchical**: several derived classes from one base.
- **Hybrid**: a combination, e.g. multilevel + multiple.
The **diamond problem**: if B and C both derive from A and D derives from B and C, D gets two copies of A. C++ solves this with a **virtual base class**: `class B : virtual public A`.
**Private members of the base are inherited but never directly accessible** in the derived class. The default inheritance mode is **private for `class`** and **public for `struct`**. Constructors, destructors, friend functions and the assignment operator are not inherited.
In Java, `class B extends A` (only one superclass) and `implements` for any number of interfaces; `super` refers to the parent. Every Java class implicitly extends **`Object`**.

Single     Multilevel   Multiple     Hierarchical
  A           A          A     B          A
  |           |           \   /          / \
  B           B             C           B   C
              |
              C
Hybrid (diamond):   A
                   / \

sections.heading: Polymorphism: compile-time vs run-time
sections.body:
**Polymorphism** means one interface, many implementations. It is of two kinds:
- **Compile-time (static, early binding)**: the call is resolved by the compiler. Achieved by **function overloading, operator overloading** and **templates**.
- **Run-time (dynamic, late binding)**: the call is resolved while the program runs, based on the actual object type. Achieved by **virtual functions** in C++ and **method overriding** in Java.
**Overloading** = same name, different parameter lists, usually in the same class. **Overriding** = a subclass redefines a method with the same signature as in the superclass.
In Java, every non-static, non-private, non-final instance method is virtual by default, so a superclass reference calls the subclass version (shown below). Static methods are not overridden; a subclass static method with the same signature **hides** the parent's. Java overriding rules: same name and parameters; return type same or a subtype (covariant); access cannot be made more restrictive; cannot override `final`, `static` or `private` methods.

sections.heading: Function overloading and operator overloading
sections.body:
**Function overloading**: several functions share a name but differ in the **number, type or order** of parameters. A different **return type alone is not enough** (compile error). Default arguments can make calls **ambiguous**, e.g. `f(int)` and `f(int, int = 0)` both match `f(5)`.
**Operator overloading** gives an existing operator a meaning for user-defined types using the keyword `operator`, e.g. `Complex operator+(const Complex&)`. Rules:
- You cannot create new operators or change an operator's **precedence, associativity or number of operands**.
- Operators that **cannot be overloaded**: `::` (scope resolution), `.` (member access), `.*` (pointer-to-member), `?:` (conditional), `sizeof` (and `typeid`).
- `=`, `()`, `[]` and `->` can be overloaded only as **member functions**.
- `<<` and `>>` for streams are normally written as **friend** functions, because the left operand is a stream, not our object.
- As a member function a **unary** operator takes 0 arguments and a **binary** operator 1; as a friend they take 1 and 2.
Java does **not** allow user-defined operator overloading; the only built-in exception is `+` for String concatenation. Java does support method overloading.

sections.heading: Virtual functions, pure virtual functions and abstract classes
sections.body:
A **virtual function** is declared with the keyword `virtual` in the base class. When it is called through a **base-class pointer or reference**, the version of the **actual object's class** runs (late binding). A non-virtual function is chosen by the **pointer's type** (early binding).
Implementation: each class with virtual functions has a **vtable**; each object holds a hidden **vptr** to it.
A **pure virtual function** has no body in the base: `virtual void draw() = 0;`. A class with at least one pure virtual function is an **abstract class**: you cannot create its objects, but you can have pointers and references to it. A derived class that does not override every pure virtual function is also abstract.
Key rules:
- **Constructors cannot be virtual**; **destructors can and should be** virtual in a base class used polymorphically, otherwise `delete basePtr` may skip the derived destructor (undefined behaviour).
- Static member functions and friend functions cannot be virtual.
- Calling through an **object** (not pointer/reference) uses static binding; assigning a derived object to a base object **slices** it.
Java equivalent: `abstract` methods and classes; an abstract class may have constructors and concrete methods.

sections.heading: Templates and exception handling in C++
sections.body:
**Templates** support **generic programming**: one definition works for many types. The compiler instantiates a version per type at **compile time** (compile-time polymorphism).
- Function template: `template <typename T> T maxOf(T a, T b)`.
- Class template: `template <class T> class Stack { T arr[50]; ... };` used as `Stack<int> s;`.
The **STL** (Standard Template Library) is built on templates: **containers** (vector, list, deque, stack, queue, map, set), **algorithms** (sort, find, reverse) and **iterators**.
**Exception handling** separates error handling from normal code using three keywords:
- `try`: block that may raise an exception.
- `throw`: raises an exception (any type: int, string, object).
- `catch`: handles it. `catch(...)` catches **every** exception and must be the last handler.
After a `throw`, control jumps to the first matching `catch`; the rest of the `try` block is skipped and local objects are destroyed (**stack unwinding**). If no handler matches, `std::terminate()` is called. C++ has no `finally`; cleanup is done by destructors (RAII).

sections.heading: Exception handling in Java
sections.body:
All Java exceptions derive from **`Throwable`**, which has two subclasses: **`Error`** (serious JVM problems such as `OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`; not normally caught) and **`Exception`**.
- **Checked exceptions** are checked by the compiler; they must be caught or declared with `throws`. Examples: `IOException`, `FileNotFoundException`, `SQLException`, `ClassNotFoundException`, `InterruptedException`.
- **Unchecked exceptions** are `RuntimeException` and its subclasses: `ArithmeticException`, `NullPointerException`, `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, `NumberFormatException`, `ClassCastException`.
Keywords: `try`, `catch`, `finally`, `throw` (raises one exception object) and `throws` (declares in the method header which exceptions it may pass on).
The **`finally`** block runs whether or not an exception occurs (it is skipped only if the JVM stops, e.g. `System.exit()`). When several `catch` blocks are used, a **subclass must be caught before its superclass**; otherwise the later block is unreachable and the code does not compile.
Do not confuse `final` (keyword), `finally` (block) and `finalize()` (deprecated garbage-collector hook).

diagram.title: Java exception hierarchy
diagram.ascii:
Object
                |
            Throwable
           /         \
       Error        Exception
         |          /        \
 OutOfMemoryError  IOException   RuntimeException
 StackOverflow-    SQLException  (unchecked)
 Error             (checked)      ArithmeticException
                                  NullPointerException

sections.heading: Java basics: features, JDK, JRE and JVM
sections.body:
Java was developed by **James Gosling** and his team at **Sun Microsystems** (originally named **Oak**). Key features: simple, object-oriented, **platform independent** ("write once, run anywhere"), architecture neutral, portable, robust (strong typing, no explicit pointers, automatic **garbage collection**), secure, multithreaded and distributed.
How a program runs:
- `javac Hello.java` compiles source into **bytecode** stored in `Hello.class`.
- `java Hello` starts the **JVM**, which loads, verifies and executes the bytecode.
- Inside the JVM: **class loader**, **bytecode verifier**, **execution engine** (interpreter + **JIT compiler** that converts frequently used bytecode to native code) and **garbage collector**.
Bytecode is platform independent; the **JVM itself is platform dependent**.
**JDK** = JRE + development tools. **JRE** = JVM + core libraries.
Entry point: `public static void main(String[] args)`. A file may hold only one `public` class, named like the file. All Java functions are members of some class and are called **methods**; they cannot be defined outside a class.

sections.heading: Java data types, operators and strings
sections.body:
Java has 8 **primitive types** with fixed sizes on every platform (see table); everything else is a reference type. Integer literals are `int` and decimal literals are `double` by default (`3.5f` for float, `10L` for long). `char` is a 16-bit **Unicode** (UTF-16) code unit, and `boolean` holds only `true`/`false` (not 0/1).
**Type promotion**: in an expression, byte, short and char are promoted to int, so `byte c = a + b;` needs a cast.
Operators to remember: `>>` (signed right shift), `>>>` (unsigned right shift, fills with 0), `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, and the short-circuit `&&`, `||`. Relational operators are `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `==`, `!=` (`=>` is not an operator). `instanceof` tests the type of an object.
**Strings**: `String` objects are **immutable**. `==` compares references; use `equals()` to compare contents. `StringBuffer` (synchronized) and `StringBuilder` (faster, not synchronized) are mutable.
`+` is evaluated **left to right**: once a String appears, later operands are concatenated as text, but numbers before the first String are added arithmetically.

sections.heading: Packages, access modifiers and interfaces in Java
sections.body:
A **package** groups related classes and interfaces and provides a namespace. `package mypack;` must be the **first statement** in the file; `import java.util.*;` or `import java.util.Scanner;` brings in classes. **`java.lang` is imported automatically** (String, Math, System, Object, Thread, wrapper classes such as Integer).
Common packages: `java.util`, `java.io`, `java.net`, `java.awt`/`javax.swing` (GUI), `java.sql`.
Important keywords: `final` (variable = constant, method = cannot be overridden, class = cannot be inherited, e.g. String), `static` (belongs to the class), `this`, `super` (`super()` must be the first statement of a constructor).
An **interface** is a fully abstract type: its methods are `public abstract` by default and its variables are `public static final` constants. Since Java 8 an interface may also contain `default` and `static` methods. A class **implements** any number of interfaces, and an interface can **extend** several interfaces, which gives Java multiple inheritance of type without the diamond problem for state.

sections.heading: Abstract class vs interface
sections.body: Neither can be instantiated with `new`. Use an **abstract class** when related classes share state and code; use an **interface** for a capability that unrelated classes share (e.g. `Runnable`, `Comparable`).

sections.heading: Multithreading in Java
sections.body:
A **thread** is a lightweight unit of execution within a process; threads of a process share its memory. Two ways to create one:
- **Extend `Thread`** and override `run()`.
- **Implement `Runnable`** (single method `run()`) and pass the object to `new Thread(r)`. Preferred, because the class can still extend another class.
`start()` creates a new thread which then calls `run()`. Calling `run()` directly just executes it in the current thread like an ordinary method. Calling `start()` twice on the same thread throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.
Life cycle (textbook): **New → Runnable → Running → Blocked/Waiting → Dead (Terminated)**. The `Thread.State` enum lists NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED.
Useful methods: `sleep(ms)` (static, keeps locks), `join()` (wait for a thread to finish), `yield()`, `isAlive()`. Priorities run from **1 (MIN_PRIORITY) to 10 (MAX_PRIORITY)**; the default is **5 (NORM_PRIORITY)**.
**Synchronization**: a `synchronized` method or block lets only one thread hold an object's lock (monitor) at a time. `wait()`, `notify()` and `notifyAll()` belong to the **Object** class, must be called while holding the lock, and `wait()` releases the lock.

formulas.note: A new thread inherits the priority of the thread that created it (main thread has 5).

workedExamples.problem: class M, class A and class B each print their name in the constructor and "~name" in the destructor. class C : public B, public A { M m; } does the same. What is printed when an object of C is created in main() and main() ends?
workedExamples.solution:
Rule: base classes are constructed in the order they are **listed in the class declaration**, then member objects in declaration order, then the body of C's constructor.
- Bases listed as B, A → B, then A
- Member object m → M
- C's own body → C
Construction: **B A M C**
Destruction is the exact reverse: **~C ~M ~A ~B**.
Note that the order in the constructor's initializer list does not change this.

Step 1 (Base → D1, protected mode): public c → protected; protected b → protected; private a → not accessible.
Step 2 (D1 → D2, public mode): protected members stay protected, so b and c are **protected** in D2; a remains **inaccessible**.
main() is outside the hierarchy, so through a D2 object it can access **none** of a, b, c.

`+` is evaluated left to right.
- 10 + 20 = 30 (both int); 30 + "Java" = "30Java"; then + 10 → "30Java10"; + 20 → **30Java1020**
- "" + 'A' = "A"; + 'B' → **AB**
- 'A' + 'B' is char + char = int: 65 + 66 = 131; 131 + "" → **131**

- p->f(): f is virtual and p points to a Q object → **Q.f**
- p->g(): g is not virtual, so the pointer type P decides → **P.g**
- r.f(): a reference also uses dynamic binding; r refers to a Q → **Q.f**
- obj.f(): obj is a P object (the Q part was sliced off when copied) → **P.f**
Output: **Q.f P.g Q.f P.f**

pitfalls: Default access is private in a C++ class but public in a struct; default inheritance mode follows the same rule.
Constructors have no return type, not even void, and can never be virtual; destructors can (and in polymorphic base classes should) be virtual.
A copy constructor must take its parameter by reference; taking it by value would require infinite recursive copying.
Functions that differ only in return type are not valid overloads.
::, ., .*, ?: and sizeof cannot be overloaded; overloading never changes precedence, associativity or the number of operands.
Calling run() instead of start() does not create a new thread in Java.
In Java == on Strings compares references; equals() compares contents.
Java has no multiple inheritance of classes, but a class can implement several interfaces.
In a Java multi-catch sequence, catching a superclass (Exception) before a subclass (ArithmeticException) is a compile-time error.
Java protected is wider than C++ protected: it also allows access from any class in the same package.
quickRevision: Three essential OOP concepts: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism (abstraction is the fourth pillar).
Simula 67 was the first OO language; Smalltalk is pure OO; C++ is hybrid.
Static data member: one copy per class, defined outside the class; static functions have no this pointer.
Construction: base → members → derived; destruction in reverse.
Diamond problem in C++ is solved by a virtual base class.
Compile-time polymorphism: overloading and templates; run-time polymorphism: virtual functions / overriding.
A class with a pure virtual function (= 0) is abstract and cannot be instantiated.
catch(...) catches all exceptions in C++; C++ has no finally block.
javac produces bytecode (.class); the JVM runs it using an interpreter and JIT compiler.
javap disassembles class files; javadoc generates HTML API documentation.
JDK = JRE + tools; JRE = JVM + libraries; JVM is platform dependent, bytecode is not.
java.lang is imported automatically; Object is the root of all Java classes.
Interface variables are public static final; methods are public abstract unless default/static.
wait(), notify() and notifyAll() are methods of Object; sleep() is a static method of Thread.

Why must a copy constructor take a reference parameter?
flashcards.back: Passing by value would call the copy constructor again, causing infinite recursion.

flashcards.front: Order of constructor calls in multilevel inheritance A → B → C?
flashcards.back: A, then B, then C; destructors run C, B, A.

flashcards.front: Which C++ operators cannot be overloaded?
What makes a C++ class abstract?
flashcards.back: At least one pure virtual function, e.g. virtual void f() = 0;

flashcards.front: Why declare a base-class destructor virtual?
flashcards.back: So that delete through a base pointer also runs the derived destructor.

flashcards.front: What is a virtual base class used for?
flashcards.back: To keep only one copy of a common base in diamond-shaped (hybrid/multiple) inheritance.
Early (static): call fixed at compile time, e.g. overloading. Late (dynamic): fixed at run time, e.g. virtual functions.
